module_title: Managing Workers and Safety on Site

lessons.title: Hiring and Training Local Youth for Moulding and Firing
lessons.body:
When you start making bricks, you need reliable helpers. Look for young people aged 18 to 30 in your village or nearby town. They are strong, eager to learn, and often unemployed. Post a notice at the market, church, or mosque, or talk to the local chief or youth leader. Ask for people who are punctual and not afraid of hard work. You do not need formal education, but basic counting and measuring helps. Start by hiring 3 to 5 workers for a small operation. Pay a fair daily wage from the first dayâdo not ask for free trial work. In many African countries, a common starting wage is 5,000 to 10,000 shillings per day (about $2â$5), depending on the region.

Training should be hands-on and short. Spend the first morning showing them how to mix clay and sand in the right ratioâusually 3 parts clay to 1 part sand for solid bricks. Demonstrate how to fill the mould, strike off excess, and turn out the brick onto a drying rack. Let each worker try while you watch and correct. For firing, teach them how to stack bricks in the kiln with gaps for air, and how to control the fire by adding wood or coal slowly. Safety during firing is criticalâshow them how to use long-handled tools and never stand directly in front of the kiln opening.

After the first week, assign one experienced worker as a team leader. Pay them a small extra allowance, like 1,000 shillings per day, to guide others. Hold a 10-minute meeting every morning to set goals: âToday we mould 500 bricksâ or âWe load 1,000 bricks into the kiln.â Check work daily and give feedback. If someone consistently makes poor bricks, retrain them instead of firing them immediately. Keep a simple attendance book and pay at the end of each week. This builds trust and reduces turnover. Remember, trained workers are your biggest assetâtreat them well and they will stay with you for years.

lessons.title: Setting Fair Wages and Working Hours
lessons.body:
Fair pay keeps your team loyal and productive. Before you hire, find out the local daily wage for casual labour. In rural areas, it might be 3,000 to 5,000 shillings; in towns, 7,000 to 15,000 shillings. Pay at least the local rate, and if possible, a little more. You can also pay by piece rate: for example, 200 shillings for every 100 bricks moulded, or 500 shillings for every 1,000 bricks stacked in the kiln. Piece rate motivates fast work, but make sure workers still earn a fair daily minimum. Never pay less than the agreed rate. Pay on timeâevery Friday or at the end of the month. If you delay, workers will leave or steal.

Working hours should be reasonable. In hot African climates, start early at 6:30 AM and finish by 2:00 PM, with a 30-minute break for tea or porridge. That is 7.5 hours of work. Avoid forcing overtime, but if you need extra bricks for a big order, offer overtime pay at 1.5 times the normal rate. For example, if the daily wage is 6,000 shillings for 8 hours, overtime is 1,125 shillings per extra hour. Provide clean drinking water and a shaded rest area. If workers must travel far, consider providing a simple lunch or a small transport allowance.

You must also handle rest days. Give one day off per week, usually Sunday, and allow workers to rest on public holidays. If they work on a rest day, pay double. Keep a written record of hours and wages for each worker. Use a notebook or a simple phone app. At the end of each month, show each worker their total pay and deductions, if any. Deductions should only be for things like advances you gave them. Never deduct for tools or mistakesâthat is your cost of doing business. When workers feel paid fairly and treated with respect, they work harder and stay longer. That saves you money on training new people and keeps your brick quality high.

lessons.title: Providing Basic Safety Gear: Gloves, Boots, and Masks
lessons.body:
Brick making is dirty and dangerous. Dust, sharp edges, and heat can hurt your workers. You must provide basic safety gear. Start with heavy-duty gloves. Leather or thick cotton gloves cost about 2,000 to 5,000 shillings per pair. They protect hands from cuts when handling rough bricks and from burns when touching hot kiln bricks. Buy one pair per worker and replace them when they get holes. Next, boots. Rubber or leather boots with steel toes are best. They cost 10,000 to 25,000 shillings per pair. They protect feet from falling bricks, sharp objects, and hot embers. Do not let workers wear sandals or flip-flops on site. If boots are too expensive, at least provide closed leather shoes.

Dust masks are also essential, especially during mixing and firing. Clay dust contains silica, which can damage lungs over time. Simple disposable masks cost 500 to 1,000 shillings each. Buy a box of 50 and give a new mask each day to workers who are mixing or near the kiln. For firing, use a mask with a filterâthese cost 5,000 to 10,000 shillings but last a month. Also provide eye protection: cheap plastic goggles cost 2,000 shillings and prevent flying chips from entering eyes. For workers near the kiln, add a heavy apron or overall to protect against sparks.

You must enforce the use of this gear. Do not allow anyone to work without gloves and boots. Keep a spare set for visitors or new workers. Set a rule: no gear, no work. If a worker refuses to wear gear, send them home without pay for that day. It sounds harsh, but it prevents injuries that could cost you more in medical bills and lost work. Also, keep a first-aid box on site with bandages, antiseptic, and burn cream. Train one worker as a safety officer to check gear daily and refill supplies. The cost of safety gear is small compared to the cost of an accident. A safe site is a productive site.

lessons.title: Preventing Injuries from Heavy Lifting and Hot Kilns
lessons.body:
Heavy lifting and hot kilns cause most injuries on brick sites. Teach your workers to lift correctly. They should bend their knees, keep their back straight, and hold the load close to their body. Never twist while lifting. For bricks, use a wheelbarrow or a hand cart instead of carrying stacks by hand. A wheelbarrow costs 30,000 to 50,000 shillings and can move 50 bricks at once. For very heavy loads, use two people or a simple pulley. Set a weight limit: no single worker should carry more than 20 kilograms alone. If a brick weighs 3 kilograms, that is about 7 bricks. Use a scale to check loads. Rotate tasks every two hours so no one does heavy lifting all day.

Hot kilns are extremely dangerous. The outside of a working kiln can reach 200Â°C or more. Never let workers touch the kiln walls with bare hands. Use long-handled tongs (at least 1 metre long) to move hot bricks. These cost 10,000 to 20,000 shillings. Workers must wear leather gloves, heavy boots, and a face shield or goggles when opening the kiln. Open the kiln slowly to let heat escape gradually. Never stand directly in front of the openingâstand to the side. Keep a bucket of water and a first-aid kit nearby. If someone gets burned, cool the burn with clean running water for 10 minutes, then cover with a clean cloth. Do not apply oil or mud.

Also prevent heat stress. Provide shade and plenty of drinking water. Workers should drink 1 cup of water every 20 minutes. Add a pinch of salt to the water to replace sweat. Work in shifts near the kiln: 30 minutes on, 30 minutes off. Watch for signs of heat exhaustion: dizziness, headache, nausea, or heavy sweating. If you see these, move the worker to a cool place, give water, and let them rest. If they faint, seek medical help. Finally, keep the site clean. Remove broken bricks and tools from walkways. Mark hot areas with warning signs. A little planning prevents painful accidents and keeps your team working.

lessons.title: Organising Work Teams for Efficient Production
lessons.body:
To make bricks efficiently, divide your workers into teams with clear roles. For a small operation of 6 to 10 workers, create three teams: mixing, moulding, and firing. The mixing team (2 people) digs clay, adds sand and water, and mixes until smooth. They should produce enough mixture for 500 bricks per day. The moulding team (3 people) fills moulds, strikes off excess, and turns out bricks onto drying racks. They can make 150 to 200 bricks per person per day. The firing team (2 people) stacks dried bricks into the kiln and controls the fire. They work in shifts because firing takes 3 to 5 days. One person can be a floater to help where needed.

Assign a team leader for each group. The leader is responsible for quality and speed. For example, the moulding leader checks that each brick is the right size and shape. The firing leader monitors temperature using a simple pyrometer or by watching the colour of the fireâbright orange is good, white is too hot. Pay team leaders an extra 1,000 to 2,000 shillings per day. Hold a 15-minute meeting every morning to set daily targets. Write the target on a board: âToday: 600 moulded, 400 stacked.â At the end of the day, count what was done. If a team meets the target, give a small bonus, like 500 shillings per person. If they miss it, find out whyâmaybe the clay was too wet or the moulds were broken.

Organise the site so teams do not get in each otherâs way. Keep clay piles near the mixing area, drying racks near the moulding area, and the kiln a safe distance away. Use a simple flow: clay â mixing â moulding â drying â firing â storage. Make sure tools are shared and returned to a central point. Have a schedule for drying: bricks need 3 to 7 days in the sun before firing. Turn them once after 2 days. With good organisation, you can increase production from 500 to 1,500 bricks per day without hiring more people. Efficient teams also reduce accidents because everyone knows their job and stays out of danger zones.

lessons.title: Keeping Workers Motivated During Peak Seasons
lessons.body:
Peak seasonsâlike before the rainy season when everyone wants bricksâput pressure on your team. You need to keep workers motivated so they do not quit or slow down. Start by paying a peak-season bonus. For example, if a worker normally earns 6,000 shillings per day, add 1,000 to 2,000 shillings per day during the busiest month. Or offer a weekly bonus of 5,000 shillings if the team meets production targets. Announce the bonus at the start of the season so everyone knows what to aim for. Also provide extra food. A hot lunch of rice and beans costs 1,500 shillings per person but gives energy and shows you care. On very hot days, bring cold water or a local drink like maas or lemonade.

Recognise good work publicly. At the end of each week, thank the team and name the top worker. Give them a small gift: a new pair of gloves, a t-shirt, or 2,000 shillings. This costs little but boosts morale. Listen to complaints. If workers say the moulds are too heavy or the kiln is too hot, fix the problem quickly. Do not ignore them. Also, rotate jobs so no one gets bored or exhausted. A moulder can switch to stacking for a day. This keeps skills sharp and reduces injuries.

Plan rest breaks. During peak season, work longer hours but give a full day off after every 10 days. If you push too hard, workers get sick or make mistakes. Provide a shaded area with benches where they can rest. Keep a radio playing music if possibleâit lifts spirits. Finally, be fair. Do not favour relatives or friends. Give everyone the same chance to earn bonuses. If you see a worker struggling, help them or pair them with a stronger worker. When the peak season ends, thank everyone and give a small end-of-season gift, like a bag of rice or 10,000 shillings. They will come back to work for you next season. Motivated workers produce more and better bricks, and your business grows.

quiz.q: What is a good starting daily wage for a brick moulding worker in many African countries?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states a common starting wage is 5,000 to 10,000 shillings per day.

quiz.q: What ratio of clay to sand is recommended for solid bricks?
options: A) 1 part clay to 3 parts sand
B) 3 parts clay to 1 part sand
C) 2 parts clay to 2 parts sand
D) 4 parts clay to 1 part sand
quiz.explanation: The lesson says to mix 3 parts clay to 1 part sand for solid bricks.

quiz.q: How often should you pay workers to build trust?
options: B) At the end of each week
D) Only when you have money
quiz.explanation: The lesson advises paying at the end of each week to build trust and reduce turnover.

quiz.q: What is a fair overtime rate if the normal daily wage is 6,000 shillings for 8 hours?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states overtime pay is 1.5 times the normal rate, so 6,000/8 = 750, times 1.5 = 1,125.

quiz.q: What should you do if a worker refuses to wear safety gear?
options: B) Send them home without pay for that day
C) Give them a warning only
D) Pay them extra to wear it
quiz.explanation: The lesson says to send them home without pay for that day to enforce safety rules.

quiz.q: Which safety gear protects hands from cuts and burns?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states heavy-duty gloves protect hands from cuts and burns.

quiz.q: What is the maximum weight a single worker should carry alone?
quiz.explanation: The lesson sets a weight limit of no more than 20 kilograms per worker.

quiz.q: How long should you cool a burn with clean running water?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says to cool the burn with clean running water for 10 minutes.

quiz.q: How many bricks can one person mould per day according to the lesson?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states a moulder can make 150 to 200 bricks per person per day.

quiz.q: What should you do if a team misses its daily production target?
options: B) Find out why and fix the problem
quiz.explanation: The lesson advises finding out why and fixing the problem instead of punishing.

quiz.q: What is a good peak-season bonus for a worker earning 6,000 shillings per day?
quiz.explanation: The lesson suggests adding 1,000 to 2,000 shillings per day during the busiest month.

quiz.q: How often should workers drink water when working near a hot kiln?
options: D) At the end of the day
quiz.explanation: The lesson says workers should drink 1 cup of water every 20 minutes.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a team leader in brick production?
options: A) To do all the work
B) To check quality and speed
quiz.explanation: The lesson says team leaders are responsible for quality and speed.

quiz.q: What should you do if a worker shows signs of heat exhaustion?
options: B) Move them to a cool place and give water
D) Send them home without pay
quiz.explanation: The lesson says to move the worker to a cool place, give water, and let them rest.

quiz.q: How long should bricks dry in the sun before firing?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states bricks need 3 to 7 days in the sun before firing.

quiz.q: What is a fair piece rate for moulding 100 bricks?
quiz.explanation: The lesson gives an example of 200 shillings for every 100 bricks moulded.

quiz.q: What should you provide for workers who travel far?
options: B) A simple lunch or transport allowance
quiz.explanation: The lesson suggests providing a simple lunch or a small transport allowance.

quiz.q: What is the best way to move 50 bricks at once?
quiz.explanation: The lesson recommends using a wheelbarrow or hand cart instead of carrying by hand.

quiz.q: What should you do before firing bricks in a kiln?
options: A) Stack them with gaps for air
quiz.explanation: The lesson says to stack bricks with gaps for air circulation.

quiz.q: How often should you hold a morning meeting with workers?
quiz.explanation: The lesson advises holding a 10-minute meeting every morning to set goals.

quiz.q: What is a good way to recognise a top worker?
options: A) Give them a small gift or bonus
quiz.explanation: The lesson suggests giving a small gift like gloves or 2,000 shillings to the top worker.

quiz.q: What should you do if a worker consistently makes poor bricks?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says to retrain them instead of firing them immediately.

quiz.q: What is the recommended length for long-handled tongs used near the kiln?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states long-handled tongs should be at least 1 metre long.

quiz.q: How many days off should a worker get during peak season?
options: B) One day off after every 10 days
quiz.explanation: The lesson advises giving a full day off after every 10 days during peak season.

quiz.q: What should you do if a worker gets a burn?
options: C) Cool with water and cover with clean cloth
quiz.explanation: The lesson says to cool the burn with clean running water and cover with a clean cloth.

quiz.q: What is a good way to keep workers motivated during peak season?
options: B) Provide extra food and bonuses
C) Increase working hours without extra pay
quiz.explanation: The lesson suggests providing extra food and bonuses to keep workers motivated.

quiz.q: What should you do if a worker complains about heavy moulds?
options: C) Tell them to work harder
quiz.explanation: The lesson says to listen to complaints and fix the problem quickly.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to lift a heavy load?
options: B) Bend your knees and keep back straight
quiz.explanation: The lesson teaches to bend the knees, keep the back straight, and hold the load close.

quiz.q: What should you keep on site for emergencies?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says to keep a first-aid box on site with bandages, antiseptic, and burn cream.

quiz.q: What is a good way to organise work teams for efficiency?
options: B) Divide into mixing, moulding, and firing teams
C) Hire one person to do all work
quiz.explanation: The lesson recommends dividing workers into mixing, moulding, and firing teams with clear roles.
